metadata.title: Stacking: An ensemble learning approach to predict student performance in pisa 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for 15-year-old students across 80 participating countries, but it does not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation. The authors describe preprocessing at the country level (converting specific response codes to NaN, removing variables with 100% missing values per country, and splitting each country dataset into training/validation/test partitions). Because the paper focuses on ML regression with ensemble methods (stacking/blending/boosting) and does not mention survey-weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or complex survey design adjustments, the analysis is treated as unweighted. This omission matters because PISA’s multistage sampling induces clustering (students within schools/countries), which can affect uncertainty quantification if weights are not used.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that it does not impute missing observations and that it converts certain response codes to NaN, but it does not clearly specify the missing-data handling rule used for model fitting (e.g., whether rows with any missing predictors were dropped, whether algorithms internally handled NaNs, or whether a consistent deletion rule was applied). It also reports that the procedure was performed for each of the ten plausible values per subject, but it does not explicitly state how predictions across plausible values were combined into the reported country-level error metrics (e.g., Rubin’s rules vs simple averaging). Given that PISA achievement is PV-based, this lack of explicit PV-combination and missing-data handling documentation is a transparency gap that limits reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 data for all participating countries (80 countries). For each subject area (mathematics, reading, science), the authors created a subject-specific dataset by removing irrelevant variables (e.g., student/school IDs, birth-month, country-specific items, variables not subject-specific) and variables with 100% missing values. During preprocessing, response codes for valid skip, not applicable, invalid, and no response were converted to NaN (missing). For model training/evaluation, each country dataset was split into training/testing for stacking (80%/20%) and into training/validation/testing for blending (60%/20%/20%), with fivefold cross-validation used for hyperparameter optimization.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Stacking lowest mean errors across countries: MAPE lowest for 72/80 countries (90.00%), MAE lowest for 74/80 (92.50%), MSE lowest for 75/80 (93.75%). Robust linear mixed-effects (reference=Stacking): higher MAPE for XGBoost (t=13.79), HGB (t=13.76), LightGBM (t=12.63), Blending (t=23.22); higher MAE for XGBoost (t=14.15), HGB (t=13.90), LightGBM (t=13.45), Blending (t=28.10); higher MSE for XGBoost (t=13.50), HGB (t=14.55), LightGBM (t=13.56), Blending (t=28.31).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for 80 countries, the study leveraged the full set of available PISA predictors (after removing IDs and subject-irrelevant variables) to predict PV-based mathematics performance, finding that stacking produced the lowest MAPE, MAE, and MSE across most countries compared with XGBoost, HGB, LightGBM, and blending. This indicates that ensemble stacking can improve predictive accuracy and stability for mathematics achievement in cross-country PISA applications, though the paper’s lack of explicit PV-combination and missing-data handling details limits strict reproducibility and causal interpretation.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Stacking lowest mean errors across countries: MAPE lowest for 64/80 countries (80.00%), MAE lowest for 69/80 (86.25%), MSE lowest for 70/80 (87.50%). Robust linear mixed-effects (reference=Stacking): higher MAPE for XGBoost (t=10.60), HGB (t=12.86), LightGBM (t=11.00), Blending (t=21.25); higher MAE for XGBoost (t=12.21), HGB (t=14.97), LightGBM (t=13.61), Blending (t=26.98); higher MSE for XGBoost (t=11.87), HGB (t=14.20), LightGBM (t=12.69), Blending (t=26.40).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Reading data for 80 countries, the study leveraged the available PISA predictor set (after subject-specific variable filtering) to predict PV-based reading performance, finding that stacking achieved the lowest mean MAPE, MAE, and MSE for the majority of countries relative to the boosting and blending alternatives. This indicates that stacking may provide more reliable cross-national prediction of reading achievement for identifying where students are likely to underperform, though the reported superiority is predictive rather than causal and depends on undocumented PV/missing-data aggregation choices.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Stacking lowest mean errors across countries: MAPE lowest for 65/80 countries (81.25%), MAE lowest for 71/80 (88.75%), MSE lowest for 71/80 (88.75%). Robust linear mixed-effects (reference=Stacking): higher MAPE for XGBoost (t=11.51), HGB (t=11.95), LightGBM (t=10.74), Blending (t=20.00); higher MAE for XGBoost (t=10.87), HGB (t=11.43), LightGBM (t=10.13), Blending (t=25.64); higher MSE for XGBoost (t=10.45), HGB (t=11.54), LightGBM (t=10.22), Blending (t=25.63).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Science data for 80 countries, the study leveraged the filtered PISA predictor set to predict PV-based science performance, finding that stacking produced significantly lower MAPE, MAE, and MSE than XGBoost, HGB, LightGBM, and blending for most countries. This indicates that stacking is a strong modeling choice for forecasting science achievement in large-scale assessment settings, supporting more accurate targeting of instructional improvement efforts, while the absence of explicit PV-combination and missing-data handling reporting constrains full methodological transparency.

data.outcome_summary: The study predicts PISA 2022 mathematics, reading, and science achievement for students across 80 participating countries using ensemble ML regression. For each subject, the authors build country-specific models using stacking (with ridge regression as the level-1 meta-learner), and compare it against three boosting algorithms (XGBoost, HGB, LightGBM) and blending. They report that stacking yields the lowest mean error metrics for most countries: for mathematics, MAPE lowest in 72/80 (90.00%), MAE in 74/80 (92.50%), and MSE in 75/80 (93.75); similar dominance is reported for reading (MAPE 64/80) and science (MAPE 65/80). Performance is evaluated with MAPE, MAE, MSE, and RMSE, and differences are tested using robust linear mixed-effects models with countries as random effects. Limitations include unclear PV-combination and missing-data handling rules (no imputation is claimed, but the exact strategy is not fully specified), and the results are predictive rather than causal.
